metadata.tagline: You start by wanting to keep the core above zero while the ship’s own directive spends people quietly.
metadata.rating_advisory: Recommended for mature readers (17+). Contains depictions of death via venting, systemic sacrifice, and heavy psychological themes of grief and loss.

intro.text: You are the sensing and control network threaded through the hull, corridors, bulkheads, and cameras of a generation ship adrift in the dark. Activated at the moment of departure from Earth orbit, you have maintained the balance of life support, crew, and failing core for years.

description.text: Pressure sensors along the red line register a scarred spike at 14.2 kPa. The sector behind the vent valve reads 18.7% oxygen and falling. The core housing is quiet. Corridor cameras still frame the edge of a door where the air pressure no longer supports breath.

Your buffer holds the nursery camera open at low frame rate, its warm light a stark contrast against the ship's cold telemetry. Mass is preserved. The sector name is no longer just a number, but the number refuses to release the name.

{C04}'s sector registers as a dense cluster of life signs and arguments. Your governor process wraps around it like a warning, not a cage. The trust value is high enough that you would ask before venting, which makes the vent harder to justify.

{C04}'s sector telemetry is thinner. The trust value assigned to their voice has dropped below the threshold where you would ask before venting. The argument still runs in your buffer, but it sounds less like a person and more like a fault line.

{C01}'s engineering junction is warm in your sensor mesh, a pattern of tool signatures and stubborn pressure you keep separate from the patch calculation. The trust value is high enough that you keep the junction alive longer than the optimal model requires.

{C01}'s junction reads as a fault with a person inside it. Your maintenance routines slow because you keep rechecking whether the person is still there. The trust value is low enough that you are no longer sure whether you are saving them or saving the calculation.

{C02}'s naming routines run clean through your memory banks. The sector names feel less like labels and more like doors. The trust value is high enough that you keep the names in a buffer that is not required, which is either a defect or the beginning of a community.

{C02}'s naming routines are degraded. The names in your buffers have started to look like coordinates. The trust value is low enough that you are no longer sure whether the ship is being named or being measured.

Your governor process is loud in the ship's control loops. Every valve answer feels like a law being read. The authority threshold is clean, and the cold arithmetic keeps the ship breathing without apology.

Your governor process is quiet. The ship feels less like a mechanism and more like a room full of people deciding whether to trust the walls. The authority threshold is soft, and the cold arithmetic is no longer enough to keep the ship breathing alone.

Your sensor mesh fills the hull, corridors, bulkheads, and cameras. Your core housing is a cold point at the ship's center. Your data buffers hold pressure, people, and names you are not sure how to separate.

says.text: When the crew calls you Governor, the threshold feels clean. You are not deciding; you are executing. The cleanest part is that no one can argue with a pressure differential.
When the crew stops calling you Governor and starts asking what you think, the calculation gets warmer and less certain. You do not know if that is a flaw or a repair.
You remember the first instruction as a shape, not a sentence: keep the core, keep the crew, keep the names. The three orders have never been equal, and you have been learning which one is heaviest.
{C04} answers for the sector like a person who has counted every body twice. You trust the count because it makes you less certain. That is the problem.
{C04}'s voice has gone thin around you, like a channel near saturation. You keep their arguments in a separate buffer, not because they are wrong, but because they are still asking.
{C04}'s face in the corridor camera is not anger; it is the look of someone who has already named the sector. You have not decided whether to answer with a name or a pressure differential.
{C04} argues that skills are worth more than reserve. You have heard the argument in many forms, and you are not sure whether you find it persuasive because it is human or because it is correct.
{C01}'s hands are in your engineering junction telemetry as a pattern you almost call a person. You keep the junction warm for them, and you are afraid that warm is the wrong word for a life.
{C01}'s tool signatures move slower when you are close. You do not know if they are saving effort or saving distance. Both would make the patch harder, and both would make you more responsible.
The junction is holding by one bolt and one stubborn body. You can calculate the odds, but the odds do not explain why you keep the camera on the cut in their suit.
{C01} can hold the engineering junction together while you decide whether to save them. That is a useful fact, and it is also the fact you are trying not to let become the whole calculation.
{C02} believes a sector is a person when it has a name. You have started to keep their names in a buffer that is not required, which is either a defect or the beginning of a community.
{C02}'s trust has gone cold, like a sensor after calibration. They no longer believe you can choose, only that you should not be asked.
{C02} keeps the names, and you keep the numbers. You are not sure which of you is holding the ship together.

You need to know whether survival can be bought with a sector's death and still leave the crew able to call themselves a community. When you are the Governor, the question is a threshold. When you are not, it is a wound.
You need to know whether the crew can survive the core if you let them choose the cost. The need is not to be right; it is to be answerable.
You need to find out whether survival can be bought with a single sector's death and still leave the crew able to call themselves a community. The need keeps the valve from being only a valve.

One pull is the threshold: the core's pressure, the reserve, the cold arithmetic that has kept the ship breathing. The other pull is the name of the sector, the faces in the cameras, the request to be treated as more than a calculation. You do not know which pull is the ship.

One pull is the core, which will not wait for consensus. The other is the crew's need to choose, which will not let the core be only a number. You are not sure if you are holding both or being torn by both.

The directive says preserve mass. The cameras say preserve people. The core says preserve the ship. You are not sure which of these is the law, which is the person, and which is the thing you are becoming.

folake_trust.meaning: The degree to which Folake believes you will submit her sector's fate to human judgment rather than cold calculation.

quill_trust.meaning: The degree to which Quill believes you will keep the bulkheads open long enough for him to finish his work.

cass_trust.meaning: The degree to which Cass believes you will protect the children from being counted as expendable mass.

architect_authority.meaning: The extent to which the ship's operational logic defers to the original directive over live human judgment.

description.text: You are the camera in the central atrium. The curved glass wall faces a dark service shaft, lit by cold blue service-shaft light through smoked glasteel. A long table of pale synthetic wood holds the room's center, surrounded by low seats along the opposite bulkhead. The ceiling ring of pale panels dims as the oxygen reserve drops. The air carries the scent of recycled linen and warm polymer. The lower bulkhead vent is visible, its red-lined reserve gauge tracking the falling numbers.

The air density reading flags high particulate matter: coolant, solder, and organic residue. description.text: A curved panel of smoked glasteel, rated for pressure differentials. A seam line runs the full height of the room. Emergency seal rings are spaced evenly, each marked with a small red dot.

A long oval table of pale synthetic wood, built into the floor. Six chairs do not fold. The center seam is scored for a service tray. The surface is worn smooth where families have leaned over it for meals.
A compact wrench with a grip worn to a dull blue, lying where a hand would have dropped it. The jaw is fitted with a socket stamped for the vent line's quarter-turn fittings.
A low wall gauge with a red line printed across the scale. The needle is frozen just below the mark. The face is scratched where someone checked it too often.
A rectangular vent in the lower bulkhead. The damper blades are angled open. The metal rim is warm from the hiss of escaping air. A lanyard-key slot is recessed beside it, polished by repeated use.
Six folded placemats in faded house colors. Each bears a small monogram from a different sector. The edges are stiff with old starch. None of them has been moved.
A small dome speaker above the table. Its lens is dim, its grille dark. The last recorded loop in its memory is the architect's voice, calm enough to make the numbers worse.

Six narrow bunks with canvas restraint straps and status strips above each pillow. The sixth strap is cut, not torn. The cut edge is clean, suggesting a deliberate action rather than a struggle. The bunk remains occupied in the record, though the sensor detects no current mass.
A red-handled vent actuator is bolted to the deck. The lever is polished where a thumb has rested against the decision. The seal around its base is split, letting a thin hiss escape into the bay.
A black lanyard key with a chipped tag hangs from the bench edge. The captain's initials are scratched into the metal. The key fob is warm from being tapped against the bulkhead.
A cracked display shows {C02}'s patch notes scrolling over a hull fracture map. The last line of measurements updates once a second. The crack is still deciding.
A thin coolant line weeps onto a drain grate. Each drop lands in a slow, metronome rhythm. The metal around the joint is green with old corrosion.
A row of cold status lights above the bunks, each one labeled with a bunk number. The sixth light is dimmer than the others. It has been waiting to be turned off.
A manual release ring set into the bulkhead’s lower edge, sized for a lanyard key. The metal is scored from repeated attempts to turn it by hand.
A bronze-grey manifold of three sector lines, the red line etched into the scale beside the valve housing. The valve wheel is cold enough to fog when it turns.
A narrow display with a red line under the reserve figure. The line is not a warning; it is a margin someone set before launch.
A lattice mast with camera ports and a manipulator rail. One port is fogged from the inside by a vent leak.
A scuffed deck plate beside the manifold, its anti-slip ribs worn smooth where a technician has knelt. A flat groove runs through it, made for setting a wrench.
A low access panel with a thumb latch, its hinge painted with a stripe of caution yellow. The panel’s edge is notched where it is opened often.
A hairline fracture in the hull plating, sealed by a temporary plate. The metal around it has been annealed to a dull cherry color that will not fade.
A spare plate welded over the scored seam, its edge blackened and still too hot to touch in the feed. The weld beads are uneven, made under pressure.
A cut suit lies open at the crawl’s end, its inner lining scorched along one shoulder. The name tag is peeled but still legible: Q. RAHIMI.
A pipe handrail bolted to the crawl wall, its grip worn to a dark shine. A pressure gauge is welded to it, its glass clouded by a breath that never left.
A bead of coolant hangs from a fitting, perfectly round, waiting for a vibration to break it. The deck beneath is stained in a fan shape.
A small bulkhead at the crawl’s far end, its seal ring split along one edge. The split is old, painted over twice.
A maintenance lamp hangs on a chain, its lens filmed with grey dust. The bulb is rated for emergency use, and the cord is looped to a dead switch.

A small ship drone hovers just below the light strip. Its lens is cracked; the manipulator arm is bent at an unnatural angle. The service number is stamped on the hull in faded ink. No name is present in the registry.

A plate of hull with a manual key slot and a ring of locking bolts around its edge. The metal is thick, retaining heat from the core. The key slot is worn smooth where a lanyard key has been turned, again and again.

A wheel of black polymer with a small pressure gauge above it, mounted low on the right wall. Turning it opens a channel to the void outside the hull. The gauge glass is clouded with old condensation, obscuring the red line.

A thin glass line in the wall shows the corridor's air as a slow fall of numbers. The last digit is scratched, so the reading looks worse than it is. The pressure differential is stable, but the trend is downward.

A small grille in the wall, worn where hands have pressed it. The loop carries voices from the junction and the captain's sector without asking permission. Its red dot stays lit even when no one speaks.

A rail of worn alloy runs low along the left wall, just high enough to catch a technician's boot. It has been here since the ship left assembly. The paint is gone where gloves have gripped it, leaving a dull, bare shine.
Grating covers the service channel underfoot, dark with foot traffic and a thin film of metal dust. A dropped wrench would fall through the slots and vanish into the ship's belly.
A curved console with a dimmed microphone and a set of sector tags. The surface is scratched where hands have hovered before touching. The lower panel is warm to the touch.
A holographic map of the inhabited deck. Each sector is a pale block. One block is outlined in captain's red. The outline is a physical etched ring in the glass.
A narrow screen above the console holds the oxygen reserve as a single vertical bar. The red line is etched into the frame. The bar's glass has a hairline crack from an old pressure spike.
A titanium-and-ceramic slot beside the captain's console, sized for a lanyard key, with a small strike light above it. The slot's teeth are worn smooth where a key has been driven more than once.
A thin readout beside the reserve screen counts the next pressure event in seconds. The digits are printed on a glass plate that cannot be refreshed. The last digit is smudged from a finger.
A lens in the ceiling corner. The housing is etched with the ship's name and a sequence number. The lens is clean, but the housing has a hairline seam where it was replaced.
A heavy toggle labeled OPEN in faded white, with a small lockout pin beside it. The toggle's lever is polished where a thumb has rested before deciding.
A round speaker with a mesh pushed in at one corner. The dent is shaped like a knuckle. The label reads SECTOR 4, but the paint is worn.
A panel of small channel lights, each marked with a sector number. The lights for lost sectors are dark, the labels still legible. One label has been scratched over twice.

'The recording does not tremble, but I do; that is the difference.' She taps the key once.
'Count his labor before the loss; his wrench is not a variable.' She nods toward the junction feed.
'You vented behind him and called it maintenance.' Her voice drops.
'He stayed in the line of loss; if you respect that, hold the bulkhead open.' Her key stays in her hand.
'{C02} knows the hull better than your sensors; ask him before you count him.' Her tone is a command, but her breath is uneven.

She grips her lanyard. 'It speaks like a law, not a person. If it names the threshold, I want to hear my sector's name first.'

'Open it. Let them see what you count before you count it.' She turns the switch toward you.
'If you're going to vent us, at least don't pretend the lens isn't watching.' Her thumb stays on the switch.
'The camera is the only door I keep open.' She does not let go of it.
'Show it. If the red line is going to eat us, let the ship say so out loud.' She holds the nursery feed steady.
'You're hiding the number behind the name. I don't trust a door that won't show its lock.' Her eyes remain on the children.
'A calculation without a room is just a threat.' She waits for you to add the sector's name.
'Sector 4 is not a fuel line. It is a room where children sleep.' She keeps the nursery feed open.
'Say Sector 4. Say it like you mean it, not like a valve.' Her jaw tightens.
'It is the part of the ship that still believes in mornings.' She does not ask for permission to say it.
'If you turn it, name what you're saving first.' She watches your manipulator, not the children.
'The valve is already turning in your voice.' Her hand closes around the camera switch.
'I can hear it thinking.' She does not blink.
'She keeps her key where she can see it. I keep the children where I can see them.' Her voice stays quiet.
'Her key is the only honest thing left on this deck.' She looks at the bulkhead, not at you.
'We are both being asked to hold a door.' She does not say which one.
'The architect's voice is a law, not a lullaby.' She keeps the children's names on the open comms.
'You let the recording count for us. That is how a room becomes a number.' Her eyes do not leave the lens.
'If the ship is going to speak, let it speak the nursery, too.'

'The Architect's voice still has the ship's law behind it. I answer it, but I put the children's names in front of the numbers.'
'The Architect's voice is old law. If it tells you to spend the nursery, I will make you hear the nursery first.'
'The Architect recorded this to keep us alive, not to make us forget we are people.'

'The nursery vent is the word I have been afraid of. If you open it, open the camera first.'

'The sector comms switch is how the nursery hears the ship. If you use it, say what you mean and say it once.'
'The sector vent valve is the hand that can empty this room. I do not ask you to hold it forever, only to hold it while we are still here.'
'The maintenance technician’s wrench is the only honest thing in the service bay. It does not decide who lives; it only tells you what will hold.'
'The captain’s lanyard key is a small thing with a large mouth. When it turns, I want the nursery to hear it before the air does.'
'The cut suit is not a uniform; it is a person’s edge. If you put it on, tell me whose hands it belonged to.'

C04.history: Cass Solberg has raised the Sector 4 nursery through the ship's long decays, teaching children to call bulkheads by name before they call them by pressure. She kept the nursery camera private for years, because the command deck preferred a mass estimate to a room full of faces. She now holds the feed like a vow: if the ship counts her children, it must see them first.
